Notes: Year Established -920 = Rehoboam's fortification of Beth-zur among the 'cities for defense in Judah' (2 Chr 11:5-7; reign c. 931-913 BCE, midpoint used; the town is also listed among Judah's towns in Josh 15:58). This encyclopedia notes a 10th-9th c. occupation gap that 'raises the question' of Rehoboam's fortification, and a large Judahite occupation in the 8th-7th c. BCE. Row event: the city 'was destroyed during Nebuchadnezzar's invasion' (c. 587/586 BCE). Destruction stated, not total abandonment, so Population blank. (Earlier Bronze Age/Hyksos settlement is not Judahite and is not counted.)

1931 newspaper report of the Sellers-Albright excavation: the town had a considerable population and was fortified under Rehoboam, and the excavators found NO evidence that Nebuchadnezzar destroyed the town during his invasion or later (contradicts the destruction claim in other sources). No figure given.

Nehemiah 3:16: 'Nehemiah the son of Azbuk, ruler of half the district of Beth-zur' repaired part of the Jerusalem wall; c. 445 BCE (Nehemiah's wall-building). Indicates a Judean administrative (half-)district seat at Beth-zur in Persian Yehud. Note: Finkelstein (2018) argues Neh 3 may reflect Hasmonean (2nd c. BCE) realities rather than the Persian period.
Archaeology: 'a small collection of evidence belongs to the Pers[ian] period of Nehemiah's day' (c. 5th c. BCE). Suggests only a modest settlement in the Persian period. No population figure.

Finkelstein, Hasmonean Realities behind Ezra, Nehemiah, and Chronicles (SBL 2018), pp. 20-21 and 53-54: Funk, P. and N. Lapp and Carter 'argued that the site was very sparsely, in fact, insignificantly inhabited in the Persian and early Hellenistic periods'; only a limited number of finds can safely be dated to the Persian period and Beth-zur 'did not yield even a single Yehud seal impression'; Stern (on a single locus) and Reich (architectural analysis) argued for significant Persian-period activity. Persian period 539-332 BCE midpoint used. Presence of at most a very small settlement; no figure.

Silver hemiobol of 'Hezekiah the governor' (yhzqyh hphh) of Persian-period Yehud found at Beth Zur (1931 excavation); coin type dated to the late 4th century BCE, 'possibly around 335 BCE' (some specialists date it slightly later, early Ptolemaic). Evidence of Judean (Yehud) provincial coinage at the site; implies some Judean activity, scale unknown.

1 Macc 4:29, 4:61: Lysias' army 'encamped at Beth-zur, and Judas met them with ten thousand men' (army sizes, not residents); after the rededication of the Temple (Dec. 164 BCE) Judas 'fortified Beth-zur, so that the people might have a stronghold that faced Idumea' (1 Macc 6:7, 6:26 also report the Jews fortified 'the sanctuary and Beth-zur'). c. 164 BCE. Beth-zur becomes a Jewish (Maccabean) fortress; no resident count.

1 Macc 6:31, 6:49-50: Antiochus V/Lysias besieged Beth-zur 'for many days'; 'He made peace with the men of Beth-zur, and they evacuated the city, because they had no provisions there to withstand a siege, since it was a sabbatical year for the land.' The king 'took Beth-zur and stationed a guard there'. c. 163/162 BCE. Jewish defenders evacuated; whether any civilians remained is not stated, so Population blank.

Josephus, Antiquities 12.9.5 (Whiston): 'the inhabitants of Bethsura were terrified at his strength; and seeing that their provisions grew scarce, they delivered themselves up on the security of oaths'; Antiochus [V] 'did them no other harm than sending them out naked. He also placed a garrison of his own in the city.' c. 162 BCE. Population 0 = the Jewish inhabitants were sent out and replaced by a Seleucid garrison per this account (ancient source; residual civilians not mentioned).
Josephus, War 1.1.5 (Whiston): Antiochus Eupator 'then took Bethsura, which was a small city'. c. 162 BCE. Indicates the scale of the settlement (a small fortified town); no figure.

1 Macc 9:52-53: the Seleucid general Bacchides 'fortified the city of Beth-zur, and Gazara, and the citadel, and in them he put troops and stores of food' (c. 160 BCE). Seleucid garrison, not a Jewish community; event row, no figure.

1 Macc 10:12-14: when the foreign garrisons of Bacchides' strongholds fled, 'Only in Beth-zur did some remain who had forsaken the law and the commandments, for it served as a place of refuge.' c. 152 BCE. Documents Hellenizing (apostate) Jews living at Beth-zur under Seleucid protection; small group, number not given.

Josephus, Antiquities 13.2.1 (Whiston): garrisons in Judea fled to Antioch 'excepting those that were in the city Bethsura, and those that were in the citadel of Jerusalem, for the greater part of these was of the wicked Jews and deserters'. c. 152 BCE. Presence of Hellenizing Jews in the Beth-zur garrison; no count.

Finkelstein (SBL 2018), pp. 21 and 85 (Table 5.1): Beth-zur was 'an important place only in the late Iron II and the late Hellenistic periods'; Table 5.1 rates activity at Beth-zur (Kh. et-Tubeiqeh) as Iron II present, Persian 'weak', Hellenistic 'strong'; sites like Beth-zur were resettled 'only in the second century BCE'. 2nd c. BCE midpoint used. Regional context (Notes only): Finkelstein estimates the whole of Judea in the 160s BCE at c. 40,000 people (p. 69). No figure for Beth-zur.

1 Macc 11:65-66: 'Simon encamped before Beth-zur and fought against it for many days'; the occupants asked for terms; 'He removed them from there, took possession of the city, and set a garrison over it.' c. 145/144 BCE. Hellenizers/Seleucid garrison removed; Hasmonean (Jewish) garrison installed, size not given.

Josephus, Antiquities 13.5.6 (Whiston): Simon besieged Bethsura, 'the strongest place in all Judea', held by a garrison of Demetrius; 'he gave them his oath, and ejected them out of the city, and he put therein a garrison of his own.' c. 144 BCE. No figure.

1 Macc 14:7, 14:33 (encomium of Simon, c. 140 BCE): Simon 'ruled over Gazara and Beth-zur and the citadel'; 'He fortified the cities of Judea, and Beth-zur on the borders of Judea, where formerly the arms of the enemy had been stored, and he placed there a garrison of Jews.' Jewish garrison town; garrison size not given (garrison, not resident count).

Coins from the excavations: 173 Seleucid (124 of Antiochus IV), 18 'Maccabean' coins and 16 coins of John Hyrcanus (r. 134-104 BCE; midpoint used). The Hasmonean coins attest Judean occupation of the town in the late 2nd c. BCE; no population figure.

'Sometime around 100 b.c. the town was abandoned' (c. 100 BCE), per the excavation results summarized in this encyclopedia. Population 0 = documented abandonment. (Encyclopaedia Judaica instead dates the destruction and abandonment to Vespasian's campaign, 68 CE - see that row.)

Encyclopaedia Judaica (M. Avi-Yonah): after the Maccabean period the city 'was destroyed and abandoned, apparently during Vespasian's campaigns' (Vespasian's Judean campaign, c. 68 CE; resettled only in the Byzantine period). Population 0 = destroyed and abandoned per this source (hedged 'apparently'; conflicts with the c. 100 BCE abandonment reported from the excavations).
